items.source: PubMed · Pakistan journal of pharmaceutical sciences
items.authors: Zhang T, Tan Y, Shan X, et al.
items.summary: Background: Dental caries are chronic infectious diseases with a high global prevalence. Its pathogenesis is closely related to the adhesion of Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans), formation of dental plaque biofilms and acid production. Currently, only a few types of anticaries drugs are available for clinical use and the long-term use of these drugs can lead to side effects, such as drug resistance and dysbiosis of the oral microbiota. Objectives: Therefore, exploring new, safe and effective anti-caries treatments is an urgent task. Screening antimicrobial drugs from herbal medicines for non-antibiotic treatment of bacteria could provide new solutions to these problems. This study aimed to…

items.title: The impact of periodontitis in cardiac autonomic dysfunction by hrv analysis.
items.authors: Vineetha S, Saravanan A, Jeyabanu M, et al.
items.summary: Introduction: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease damaging the supportive structure of teeth. It has systemic impacts including cardiac autonomic dysfunction. Heart Rate Variability (HRV) measures an objective analysis of the extent of autonomic regulation and where decreased parasympathetic activity coupled with increased sympathetic predominance was determined to correlate well with risk in cardiovascular events. This research ascertains periodontitis and its correlation to autonomic dysfunction by HRV analysis. Methodology: In total, 54 periodontitis patients were involved in the study, categorized under four groups, namely Gingivitis (n=14), Mild Periodontitis (n=13),…

items.authors: Ali S, Ayub SA, Ahmad S, et al.
items.summary: Background: Professionalism in dentistry extends beyond technical competence to include accountability, respect for patients and colleagues, non-maleficence, informed consent, communication, fairness, and conduct consistent with professional standards. In Pakistan, these expectations are shaped by international bioethical principles, national professional regulation, and local social and religious contexts. Aim: To explore undergraduate dental students' experiences of, or observations of, events they perceived as unethical or inconsistent with professional conduct during clinical/workplace learning, and to understand the forms and meanings of these experiences. Methods: A qualitative…

items.title: Cystathionine beta-synthase alleviates intervertebral disc degeneration by inhibiting ferroptosis of nucleus pulposus cells via the PI3K-AKT Axis.
items.authors: Yang CJ, Hu HF, Yang Y, et al.
items.summary: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is the leading cause of low back pain, affecting 619 million people worldwide in 2020, yet no effective disease-modifying therapy is clinically available to reverse its progression. Ferroptosis has been proven to be a core driver of IVDD by inducing injury to nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs). The regulatory role of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) in IVDD and its underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the biological function of CBS in IVDD and elucidate the mechanism by which it regulates NPC ferroptosis. We found that CBS expression was significantly downregulated in degenerated human NP tissues and rat IVDD models…

Digital images of three dental offices - simple, intermediate, and luxurious were generated by artificial intelligence and evaluated through a questionnaire comprising six domains: trust, quality of care, hygiene and safety, furniture and equipment, technological updates, and recommendation. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, chi-square,…

items.title: Autologous Conditioned Serum Improves Early Wound Healing Scores of Postextraction Dental Wound in Dogs.
items.authors: Šakarnytė L, Matsuzaki I, Troillet J, et al.
items.summary: This retrospective study evaluated the potential role of autologous conditioned serum (ACS) as an adjunctive therapy to improve postextraction dental wound healing in dogs. Clinical records of 40 dogs that underwent tooth extraction were included in the analysis. Data from 20 dogs that had received ACS applied to the extraction site following suturing were compared with those from 20 dogs that received the standard treatment. Healing outcomes were assessed from follow-up notes at days 3, 7 and 14, using the Early Wound Healing Score (EHS) to evaluate haemostasis, inflammation, and wound margin closure. Analysis revealed that dogs treated with ACS demonstrated significantly higher EHS…

items.title: Endodontic-Periodontal Lesions: Biological Basis, Diagnostic Challenges, and Contemporary Management Strategies.
items.authors: Mallya L, Roma M, Shetty K, et al.
items.summary: The dental pulp and periodontium are intimately connected through anatomical structures such as the apical foramen, lateral and accessory canals, and dentinal tubules, creating pathways for the bidirectional spread of infection and inflammation. This close relationship can result in endodontic-periodontal lesions, which often present significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to overlapping clinical and radiographic features. This review aims to examine the etiopathogenesis, classification, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management approaches for endodontic-periodontal lesions. A narrative review of classical and current literature was conducted, focusing on the…

items.title: Surface-Engineered pH-Responsive Cobalt Sulfide Nanozyme for Caries Therapy.
items.authors: Wang T, Jin Y, Liu S, et al.
items.summary: Dental caries is driven by acidogenic biofilms embedded in an extracellular polymeric substance matrix, which shelters inner bacteria and diminishes antimicrobial efficacy. Nanozyme-based catalytic therapy is a promising alternative, whereas the inadequate catalytic performance coupled with weak interaction with bacteria severely limits the therapeutic efficacy. In this study, a pH-responsive polyethyleneimine-engineered cobalt sulfide (PCoS) nanozyme with a positive charge was developed, exhibiting enhanced oxidase- and peroxidase-like dual activities that were selectively initiated under acidic conditions. PCoS nanozyme effectively adsorbed onto bacterial surfaces, killed planktonic…

items.authors: Hage J, Fields HW, Johnston WM, et al.
items.summary: Objectives: This cross-sectional study investigated factors associated with pretreatment patient attrition in an advanced education orthodontic clinic. Materials and methods: Clinical records of 1567 patients attending screening and 829 patients attending records appointments in 2022-2024 were accessed. Attrition, the dependent variable, was defined as discontinuation of care despite a recommendation to proceed. Independent variables included patient's age, gender, home-to-clinic distance, case category, insurance type, prospect of Medicaid coverage, case complexity, recommended treatment plan and appliance, and time between screening and records appointments. items.title: Engineering a 3D microfluidic platform to model neuroimmune interactions in periodontal inflammation.
items.authors: Menon N, Ali A, Shrestha A, et al.
items.summary: Neuroimmune interactions play a critical role in the progression of periodontal inflammatory diseases such as apical periodontitis (AP), highlighting the need for in vitro systems capable of capturing their multicellular complexity within physiologically relevant microenvironments. Here, we present a novel 3D tri-culture microfluidic platform (3TMP) that integrates human periodontal ligament cells (PDLCs) and macrophages (MQs) in collagen 1 matrix, and neuron-like cells (NLCs) in Matrigel to investigate coupled immune, stromal, and neuronal signaling. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation induced temporally distinct inflammatory responses within the device. These responses were notably…

items.title: Periodontal Infectogenomics in Africa: The Biological Case for a Population-Centred Research Agenda.
items.authors: Kabbashi S, Chetty M
items.summary: African populations harbour the greatest human genetic diversity on earth and carry the highest global burden of severe periodontitis, yet their absence from periodontal infectogenomics represents a biological limitation of the field with profound implications for host-microbe interaction research. This Perspective builds the biological case for African populations as an urgent research priority and proposes a research roadmap integrating genomics, metagenomics and multiomics approaches.

items.authors: Eliasz W, Gawriołek M, Urbanowicz T, et al.

This systematic review aimed to synthesize existing evidence regarding dental caries burden, measured by decayed, missing, and filled teeth (DMFT), among individuals with coronary artery disease. This narrative review examines contemporary therapeutic approaches in the context of diagnosis, pathogenesis, prevalence, and patient-related and local risk modifiers. items.summary: In periodontitis, recalcitrant biofilms and the vicious endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-ROS-inflammation cycle cause persistent inflammatory osteolysis. However, current treatments mainly alleviate infection and inflammation, without targeting this ER stress-centered etiological circuit. Herein, we report the de novo design of an ER-regulating heterojunction (ERR-HJ), composed of cobalt selenide (CoSe), Ti 3 C 2 MXene, and taurine, for periodontitis treatment via bacterial clearance, ER homeostasis maintenance, and alveolar bone regeneration. items.authors: Sales-Junior RO, Dal-Fabbro R, Cardoso LM, et al.
items.summary: Oral, craniofacial, and dental tissues differ in developmental origins, healing capacity, and immunological niche, and these differences complicate functional regeneration. Healing across the craniomaxillofacial, periodontal, and pulp-dentin systems frequently results in fibrotic repair rather than true regeneration, an outcome decisively shaped by the surrounding inflammatory microenvironment. items.title: Evaluating shared gene prioritization for type 2 diabetes and FinnGen R10 chronic periodontitis.

Many teenage health problems—eating disorders, smoking, drug use, sexually transmitted diseases—can be uncovered by examining their mouth, teeth and gums, the AAP says in a clinical report titled "Oral Health for Adolescents."

items.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

items.summary: The causal role of occlusal factors, particularly malocclusion and dental attrition, in temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) remains unclear because of inconsistent observational evidence and confounding influences, limiting definitive conclusions regarding their independent etiological contributions.

items.title: Jawbone necrosis in advanced breast cancer: Study highlights the importance of oral health
items.summary: Antiresorptive drugs, which reduce bone breakdown, are an important part of treatment for breast cancer that has spread to the bones. However, their use can be associated with medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), a condition in which bone tissue in the jaw dies. In a Finnish registry study, osteonecrosis of the jaw was diagnosed in 12.6% of patients treated with denosumab during long-term follow-up.

items.title: Periodontitis and Oral Cancer Risk.
items.source: PubMed · Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America
items.authors: Mehrnia N, Sonis S
items.summary: An association between periodontitis and oral cancer risk and progression has been suggested. It seems most likely that periodontitis plays an indirect role in oral cancer risk and progression in which its contribution to a chronic inflammatory state characterized by the persistent release of pro-inflammatory cytokines contributes to oxidative stress and DNA damage, potentially favoring carcinogenic processes. Periodontal health status of an individual may serve as a surrogate for general health as those factors which contribute to good general health, environment, lifestyle, and access to care are also determinants of oral health and impact cancer risk.

items.title: Intravital 3-photon microscopy of leukocyte dynamics in the splenic white pulp.
items.authors: Schienstock D, Devi S, Mueller SN
items.summary: Intravital imaging has been instrumental in uncovering the complex behaviors of immune cells during immune responses against viruses and tumors. The spleen is a major hub for systemic immune responses and immune memory. items.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Scientists restore two hours of sleep without clearing brain plaques
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: the brain’s own immune cells. In mice with amyloid plaques, overactive microglia triggered inflammation that kept the brain from getting enough deep, restorative sleep. Temporarily removing most of these cells restored more than two hours of sleep per day, even though the plaques remained unchanged.

items.title: A secret cell alliance may explain why ovarian cancer is so deadly
items.summary: Scientists have discovered why ovarian cancer spreads so rapidly through the abdomen. Cancer cells enlist normally protective abdominal cells, forming mixed groups that work together to invade new tissue. These helper cells lead the way, allowing cancer to spread faster and resist chemotherapy. The findings uncover a critical weakness that future treatments may target.

items.title: Why Studying Human Nerves Could Unlock Better Treatments for Chronic Pain
items.summary: Read about two NIDCR researchers who are studying what goes wrong in the nervous system during chronic pain. Their focus is on two common but very different pain conditions: diabetic painful neuropathy (DPN) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

items.title: Multiple nodules in the oral cavity
items.summary: A 42-year-old Hispanic woman sought treatment for several widely distributed soft-tissue nodules involving the tongue and buccal mucosa. She first noticed the lesions approximately 5 months previously. She reported transient discomfort on the left side of the tongue 3 months earlier but was otherwise asymptomatic. Her medical history was unremarkable; she was healthy, was not taking any medications, and denied…

items.title: This natural amino acid could help stop cavities before they start
items.summary: Sugar-loving mouth bacteria create acids that damage teeth, but arginine can help fight back. In a clinical trial, arginine-treated dental plaque stayed less acidic, became structurally less harmful, and supported more beneficial bacteria. These changes made the biofilms less aggressive after sugar exposure. The results point to arginine as a promising, natural addition to cavity-prevention strategies.

items.title: Mechanical Memory and NF-κB Signaling in Dental Pulp Stem Cell Odontogenic Differentiation
items.summary: This study aimed to investigate how substrate stiffness and dimensionality regulate stemness, senescence, and subsequent odontogenic differentiation in dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs). It further examines the interplay of priming period and odontogenic induction and elucidates the role of NF-κB signaling in this process.

items.title: An enlarging pigmented lesion of the bilateral hard palatal mucosa
items.summary: An 84-year-old woman came to our oral medicine and oral oncology clinic for evaluation of a pigmented lesion of the bilateral palatal mucosa (Figure 1) that had increased in size over the prior 3 months. At the time of consultation, she reported the right hard palatal mucosa as having had a stable pigmented lesion for 11 years. After the initial discovery at that time by her dentist, a biopsy by her otolaryngologist…

items.title: Harmful mouth bacteria may trigger Parkinson’s disease
items.summary: A familiar mouth bacterium best known for causing cavities may also be quietly influencing the brain. Scientists found that when this microbe settles in the gut, it produces compounds that can travel through the bloodstream and harm neurons involved in movement. In animal studies, this process triggered inflammation, motor problems, and brain changes linked to Parkinson’s disease. The findings hint that protecting…

items.title: A smarter way to screen for breast cancer is emerging
items.summary: A groundbreaking study shows that breast cancer screening works better when it’s personalized. Instead of annual mammograms for all, women were screened based on genetics, health history, and lifestyle factors. This approach reduced advanced cancers without increasing risk for those screened less often. Most women preferred the personalized model, hinting at a major shift in future screening guidelines.

items.title: With the Rise of Right‐Wing Governments, Why a One‐Time “50% Health Tax” Will Be a Hard Sell and How It Could Be Implemented
items.summary:
ABSTRACT

items.summary: Dear WFO Fellows, With a heart full of joy and gratitude, I extend my warmest wishes to you for a happy, healthy, and inspiring New Year. As we close one remarkable chapter and step into the next, I am deeply moved by the dedication, passion, and unity each of you brings to our global WFO family. This past year has been truly extraordinary because of you. Together, we shared memorable moments at the Global Educators…

items.title: A new way to prevent gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
items.summary: Scientists are uncovering a surprising way to influence bacteria—not by killing them, but by changing how they communicate. Researchers studying oral bacteria found that disrupting chemical signals used in bacterial “conversations” can shift dental plaque toward healthier, less harmful communities. The discovery could open the door to new treatments that prevent disease by maintaining a balanced microbiome rather…

items.title: 3D Educational Animations
items.summary: Introducing a new animation series designed to support educators in enhancing their curriculum! The Academy has developed highly realistic virtual visualizations of foundational periodontal concepts that closely reflect clinical practice. New animations will be released every few months, covering a wide range of topics—from Periodontal Anatomy and Peri-implant Tissues to Measuring Gingival and Tooth Mobility, and…

items.title: International teaching service helps advance orthodontic patient care in many countries
items.summary: E arly in my career I was interested in volunteering overseas as an orthodontist. Most of the oral health volunteer opportunities, however, were for general dentists and oral surgeons. There are now options available to share our clinical expertise in orthodontics with overseas colleagues through teaching. Health Volunteers Overseas (HVO) is a private, non-profit, volunteer organization that was founded in 1986. HVO…

items.summary: The global symposium of the Society of Orthodontic Specialty Certifying Boards took place during the 10 th IOC in Rio de Janeiro on October 22, 2025. P articipants including orthodontic board presidents, examiners from multiple orthodontic boards worldwide as well as interested orthodontic practitioners participated in round table discussions moderated by assigned orthodontic leaders. Dr. Roberto Hernandez Orsini,…

items.summary: J oining WFO President Dr. Letizia Perillo in leading the organization during the next five years will be an outstanding team of orthodontists. They join returning Executive Committee members, with everyone eager to work to advance the specialty worldwide. “I am truly delighted towelcome our new Executive Committee members.” – Dr. Letizia Perillo “It is a great honor and joy to begin this journey with such talented,…

items.title: Garlic mouthwash shows shockingly strong germ-fighting power
items.summary: Garlic extract is emerging as a surprisingly powerful contender to chlorhexidine, the long-standing “gold standard” in antimicrobial mouthwashes. A systematic review of clinical studies shows that higher-concentration garlic mouthwash can rival chlorhexidine in killing bacteria—sometimes outperforming it—while offering a more natural alternative.

items.title: Podcast: Clinical Matters - The European Association for Osseointegration EAO
items.summary: The EAO podcast brings you closer to the science behind implant dentistry, translating cutting-edge research into practical insights.

items.title: Boosting one protein helps the brain protect itself from Alzheimer’s
items.summary: Researchers discovered that raising the protein Sox9 can help the brain’s astrocytes clear out toxic plaque buildup linked to Alzheimer’s. In mouse models that already showed memory problems, activating these cells improved cognitive performance. The treatment also reduced plaque levels over time. The work points toward a natural, cell-based way to slow Alzheimer’s decline.

items.title: Everyday microplastics could be fueling heart disease
items.summary: Microplastics—tiny particles now found in food, water, air, and even human tissues—may directly accelerate artery-clogging disease, and new research shows the danger may be far greater for males. In mice, environmentally realistic doses of microplastics dramatically worsened plaque buildup, altered key vascular cells, and activated harmful genes linked to inflammation and atherosclerosis, all without changes to…

items.title: Goodbye cavities? This new toothpaste made from hair can heal enamel
items.summary: Scientists have found that keratin, the protein in hair and skin, can repair and protect tooth enamel. The material forms a mineralized layer that halts decay and restores strength, outperforming traditional fluoride. Made from sustainable sources like hair, it could soon be available in toothpaste or gels. The discovery could transform dentistry by turning waste into a powerful tool for regeneration.

items.title: New gel regrows tooth enamel and could transform dentistry
items.summary: Researchers have created a bioinspired gel that can regenerate tooth enamel by mimicking natural growth processes. The fluoride-free material forms a mineral-rich layer that restores enamel’s strength and structure while preventing decay. It can even repair exposed dentine and reduce sensitivity. Early testing shows it performs like natural enamel, with potential for rapid clinical use.

items.title: Wegovy in a pill? Massive weight loss results revealed
items.summary: Novo Nordisk’s oral semaglutide 25 mg achieved up to 16.6% weight loss in a landmark study, rivaling injectable Wegovy. The pill also improved cardiovascular risk factors and physical activity levels. With a safety profile consistent with existing treatments, experts see it as a breakthrough for patients preferring oral options.

items.title: Gum disease may quietly damage the brain, scientists warn
items.summary: People with gum disease may have higher levels of brain white matter damage, a new study finds. Researchers observed that participants with gum disease had significantly more white matter hyperintensities, even after accounting for other risk factors. The findings hint that chronic oral inflammation could subtly impact the brain, especially in older adults. More research is needed, but keeping gums healthy might…

items.title: Cavities and gum disease could nearly double stroke risk
items.summary: People with both cavities and gum disease were found to have an 86% higher stroke risk than those with healthy mouths. The study followed thousands of adults for two decades, linking poor oral health with major cardiovascular events. Regular dental checkups dramatically reduced these risks, hinting that simple oral care could play a vital role in stroke prevention.

items.title: Exercise and omega-3s could be the secret to healthier teeth
items.summary: Researchers found that combining regular exercise with omega-3 supplements can make a big difference for oral health. The duo helps the immune system fight off chronic tooth root infections and reduces bone loss around the teeth. In animal studies, those that both exercised and took omega-3s had much lower inflammation and healthier bone structure.
